entry.title: Supervised Learning
entry.content:
Supervised learning is one of the fundamental paradigms of machine learning. In essence, it consists of training a model using labeled data, that is, data in which both the inputs (features) and the correct outputs (labels or targets) are known. The model learns to map inputs to outputs by identifying patterns and relationships in the data.

This process resembles a student learning under the supervision of a teacher: the model is presented with examples and their correct answers, and learns to generalize in order to correctly predict new inputs.

How does it work?

Supervised learning operates with a labeled dataset, where each ‘point’ of information includes an input (the features) and its expected output (the label). The objective of the model is to learn a mapping — a mathematical function — that transforms those inputs into the correct outputs. Thus, when the model sees new inputs it has never seen before, it will be able to predict their output with high accuracy.

Phases of Supervised Learning

Training Phase

The model receives many input-output pairs. It learns a function that approximates the relationship between them.

Prediction Phase

Once trained, the model receives new inputs (without labels) and generates predictions based on what it has learned.

The data is usually divided into:

  • Training Set (70–80%): To learn the patterns.
  • Validation Set (10–15%): To adjust hyperparameters.
  • Test Set (10–15%): To evaluate the final performance of the model.

Key Concepts

  • Input Features (Features/X): Attributes used by the model to make predictions.
  • Labels (Labels/Targets/y): Expected results the model must learn to predict.
  • Loss Function (missing term): Error between predictions and the actual labels.
  • Generalization: The model’s ability to make correct predictions on new data.

Types of Supervised Learning

Classification

The model predicts discrete categories.

Regression

The model predicts continuous numerical values.

Structured Prediction

The model predicts complex outputs, such as sequences or structures.

Challenges of Supervised Learning

Overfitting:

The model learns the training data too well, memorizing the “noise” instead of the general patterns.

Underfitting:

The model is too simple to capture relevant patterns in the dataset. It fails to learn adequately from both training and new data.

In the next article of this series, we will dive into some of the most popular supervised classification algorithms and implement them step by step with Python, so you can see them in action and start building your own models!

Stay tuned!

entry.title: What is Machine Learning?
entry.content:
Machine Learning (ML) is a fundamental branch of Artificial Intelligence (AI) that enables computers to learn from data and experiences without being explicitly programmed for each specific task. This learning capability is achieved through algorithms capable of uncovering hidden patterns within large volumes of information, continually adjusting their internal parameters to make accurate predictions and intelligent decisions.

Arthur L. Samuel defined machine learning in 1959 as “the field that gives computers the ability to learn without being explicitly programmed.” While ML utilizes statistical techniques, its primary focus is precise prediction and effective generalization to previously unseen data, distinguishing it from traditional statistics, which primarily emphasizes explanation and estimation of relationships.

Essentially, ML functions by identifying mathematical patterns within historical data. Once a model learns these patterns, it can apply them to predict or classify future data.

In practice, Machine Learning enables computers to make reliable predictions from data. However, its application is not limited to predictive analysis alone, as its primary objective is to understand data and utilize this knowledge to accurately automate complex tasks.

Types of Machine Learning

Machine Learning algorithms are classified based on the way they learn from data:

  • Supervised Learning: The model learns using labeled data to predict specific outcomes.
  • Unsupervised Learning: Identifies structures and patterns within datasets that are not labeled.
  • Reinforcement Learning: The model learns through trial and error, receiving rewards or penalties based on its actions.
  • Semi-Supervised Learning: Combines a small set of labeled data with a large quantity of unlabeled data to enhance learning accuracy.
  • Others (Ensemble, Federated, etc.): Combines multiple models or applies techniques that allow models to be trained in a decentralized manner, respecting data privacy.

Machine Learning is a rich ecosystem of learning paradigms that address different types of problems and data.

In this article, we laid the groundwork for understanding what Machine Learning is and why it matters. In the next article, we’ll explore Supervised Learning, where models learn from labeled data — and build our first real predictive models in Python.

Whether you’re just getting started or revisiting your foundations, this series will walk you through practical machine learning with clarity and code.

Stay tuned — and feel free to connect or leave a comment

This theme implements a built-in Jekyll feature, the use of Rouge, for syntax highlighting. It supports more than 100 languages. This example is in C++. All you have to do is wrap your code in markdown code tags:

```c++
code code code
```

int main(int argc, char const \*argv[])
{
    string myString;

    cout << "input a string: ";
    getline(cin, myString);
    int length = myString.length();

    char charArray = new char * [length];

    charArray = myString;
    for(int i = 0; i < length; ++i){
        cout << charArray[i] << " ";
    }

    return 0;
}

For displaying code in a list item, you have to be aware of the indentation, as stated in this FAQ. You must indent your code by (3 * bullet_indent_level) spaces. This is because kramdown (the markdown engine used by Jekyll) indentation for the code block in lists is determined by the column number of the first non-space character after the list item marker. For example:

1. We can put fenced code blocks inside nested bullets, too.

   1. Like this:

      ```c
      printf("Hello, World!");
      ```

   2. The key is to indent your fenced block in the same line as the first character of the line.

Which displays:

  1. We can put fenced code blocks inside nested bullets, too.

    1. Like this:

      printf("Hello, World!");

    2. The key is to indent your fenced block in the same line as the first character of the line.

By default, it does not display line numbers. If you want to display line numbers for every code block, you can set kramdown.syntax_highlighter_opts.block.line_numbers to true in your _config.yml file.

If you want to display line numbers for a specific code block, all you have to do is wrap your code in a liquid tag:

{% highlight c++ linenos %}
code code code
{% endhighlight %}
